titles.l2: Finding one that breaks the rule

kernelIdea: ¬(∀x p(x)) is the same as ∃x ¬p(x), and ¬(∃x p(x)) is the same as ∀x ¬p(x). A single counterexample destroys a universal claim.

kernels.l1: To knock down an every claim, find one bad apple. Just one is enough.
kernels.l2: The opposite of an every telling is a some telling: one bad apple breaks it. The opposite of a some telling is an every telling: you have to check them all.
kernels.l3: The opposite of "every case works" is "some case fails," and the opposite of "some case works" is "every case fails." So one bad apple — a single counterexample — is enough to destroy a for all claim.
kernels.l4: Denying "every x has the property" gives "some x lacks it", and denying "some x has it" gives "every x lacks it". So one counterexample refutes a *for all* claim outright.
kernels.l5: Negating a quantified statement swaps *for all* with *there exists* and negates what follows. With nested quantifiers the swap happens at every level.
kernels.l6: Pushing a denial inward through a quantified statement flips each quantifier in turn and negates what is left at the end. The *there exists* it produces is exactly the one bad apple you go hunting.
kernels.l7: Negation exchanges the two quantifiers and passes to the negated property — De Morgan's laws with the chain run out forever. So refuting a *for all* statement means exhibiting a single counterexample.
kernels.l8: Denying *for every* gives *there is*, and denying *there is* gives *for every*, with the denial pushed inward. That is why one counterexample refutes a universal claim and why refuting an existence claim takes an argument about everything.
